guidance: Take Iron-Folic Acid (IFA) tablets daily as prescribed — these are free at Anganwadi and PHC centers under government programs. Eat iron-rich foods: spinach, moringa leaves, black gram, eggs, fish, and jaggery. Drink lemon water with meals to boost iron absorption. Severe anemia in pregnancy requires immediate medical attention and may need iron infusions.
precautions: Do not skip IFA tablets — take even if they cause mild nausea (take after meals)
Avoid tea or coffee within 1 hour of taking iron tablets as they block absorption
Consume Vitamin C rich foods (amla, guava, lemon) alongside iron-rich meals
Report severe breathlessness or palpitations to doctor immediately
Attend all Antenatal Care (ANC) checkups for hemoglobin monitoring

symptoms: sudden swelling of face, hands, or feet
nausea and vomiting in late pregnancy
guidance: This is a medical emergency. Go to the nearest government hospital or CHC immediately. Do not attempt home management. Preeclampsia can rapidly progress to eclampsia (seizures) and threaten both mother and baby's life. Monitoring blood pressure at every ANC visit is crucial for early detection.
precautions: Attend all ANC checkups without fail — BP is checked each visit
Report sudden swelling, headache, or visual changes to ASHA or doctor immediately
Avoid self-medicating with any BP drugs during pregnancy
Low-dose aspirin may be prescribed by doctor from 12 weeks in high-risk cases — take as prescribed

symptoms: generalized tonic-clonic seizures in a woman with preeclampsia
can occur during pregnancy, labor, or postpartum
guidance: MEDICAL EMERGENCY — Call 108 immediately. Eclampsia is a leading cause of maternal death. Treatment: IV magnesium sulfate (anticonvulsant) and antihypertensives. Immediate delivery is often needed. Do not attempt to stop the seizure at home — protect the woman from injury during the seizure.
precautions: Magnesium sulfate is the drug of choice — give at the first sign of seizure
Monitor urine output, respiratory rate, and knee reflexes
Do not give any oral medicines if seizure is active

guidance: Diagnosed through oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) usually between 24-28 weeks. Manage with diet: avoid sugar, white rice, refined flour; eat high-fiber foods, whole grains, vegetables. Monitor blood sugar at home if advised. Some cases need insulin during pregnancy. Usually resolves after delivery but increases future risk of Type 2 diabetes.
precautions: Attend glucose screening test at 24-28 weeks of pregnancy
Avoid sweet drinks, sugary snacks, and processed foods
Exercise gently (walking 20-30 min daily) if no complications — consult doctor first
Get blood sugar tested again 6-8 weeks after delivery

symptoms: heavy vaginal bleeding after delivery (soaking more than 1 pad per hour)
guidance: This is a life-threatening emergency. Call 108 immediately and get to the nearest hospital with blood bank facilities. PPH is the leading cause of maternal death in India. Every woman should deliver in an institution where this can be managed. Oxytocin is given routinely after delivery to prevent PPH at government facilities.
precautions: Deliver in a government hospital or health facility — do NOT plan home delivery
Inform doctors of any clotting disorders or history of PPH
Know your blood group before delivery
Arrange blood donors from family before due date
ASHA worker or 108 ambulance should be pre-alerted near due date

category: Morning Sickness (Nausea and Vomiting in Pregnancy)
symptoms: vomiting (can occur any time of day)
guidance: Usually peaks between 6-12 weeks and improves by 14-16 weeks. Eat small frequent meals every 2 hours. Keep dry crackers or biscuits nearby to eat before getting out of bed. Ginger tea, lemon water, or cold plain foods may help. Avoid spicy or strong-smelling foods. Severe vomiting (hyperemesis gravidarum) with inability to keep fluids down needs hospital treatment with IV fluids.
precautions: Eat small amounts frequently rather than large meals
Avoid lying down immediately after eating
Stay hydrated — sip ORS or coconut water if unable to drink much
Seek hospital care if unable to keep any food or fluids down for more than 24 hours
Do not take any anti-nausea medications without doctor's prescription

symptoms: inability to keep food or fluids down
dehydration (dry mouth, decreased urine, sunken eyes)
guidance: This is a serious condition requiring hospital admission. Treatment: IV fluids, electrolyte correction, thiamine supplementation, antiemetics (ondansetron, promethazine). Do not delay — it can lead to Wernicke's encephalopathy and severe weight loss. Early treatment is key.
precautions: Seek care if you cannot keep any food/water down for 24 hours
Do not stop taking prenatal vitamins without consulting
Small frequent meals with bland foods

symptoms: sharp stabbing pain on one side of abdomen
vaginal bleeding (may be light or heavy)
positive pregnancy test with these symptoms
guidance: This is a medical emergency. The fertilized egg has implanted outside the uterus (usually in fallopian tube). If the tube ruptures, internal bleeding is life-threatening. Go to the emergency room immediately. Treated by surgery or medication depending on how early it is caught.
precautions: Get an early ultrasound at 6-8 weeks to confirm intrauterine pregnancy location
Report any pain or bleeding in early pregnancy to a doctor immediately
Women with history of ectopic pregnancy, PID, or tubal surgery are at higher risk
Do not delay seeking care if sharp abdominal pain occurs in early pregnancy
Call 108 and go directly to a hospital with surgical facilities

symptoms: cramping or pain in lower abdomen or back
passage of tissue or clots from vagina
guidance: Seek medical care for any bleeding in pregnancy. Early miscarriage (before 12 weeks) is common and often occurs due to chromosomal abnormalities — it is not the mother's fault. Hospital evaluation confirms complete vs incomplete miscarriage. Incomplete miscarriage needs medical or surgical management. Emotional support and grief counseling are equally important.
precautions: Do not attempt to manage miscarriage at home — go to hospital
All bleeding in pregnancy needs medical evaluation
Do not insert anything into vagina during bleeding
Wait at least 2-3 menstrual cycles before trying to conceive again (as advised by doctor)
Seek counseling support — miscarriage causes significant grief and loss

symptoms: persistent sadness or crying after childbirth
extreme fatigue beyond normal new-parent tiredness
difficulty sleeping even when baby sleeps
thoughts of harming self or baby
guidance: PPD is a medical condition — not a sign of weakness or bad motherhood. It affects 1 in 5 new mothers. Talk to a doctor or ANM at your health center. Counseling and support groups help greatly. In moderate-severe cases, medication may be needed (safe during breastfeeding if prescribed). Strong family support and sharing baby care responsibilities are key to recovery.
precautions: Screen all new mothers at 2 weeks and 6 weeks postpartum for depression symptoms
NEVER leave mother alone if she expresses thoughts of harming herself or baby — seek emergency help
Family members should actively share baby care to prevent exhaustion
Do not dismiss postpartum mood changes as 'just hormones' — seek medical evaluation
SNEHI helpline: 91529-87821 for mental health support

symptoms: red, warm, swollen area on one breast
guidance: Continue breastfeeding — stopping abruptly worsens mastitis. Nurse frequently to drain the affected breast. Apply warm compresses before feeding and cold compress after. Antibiotics are usually needed — consult a doctor. Most women recover fully within 10 days with proper treatment. If a lump remains with fever, abscess may have formed requiring drainage.
precautions: Do not stop breastfeeding — continue feeding from affected breast
Ensure baby is latching correctly — poor latch causes nipple damage and mastitis
Wear supportive but not tight-fitting bras
Complete the full antibiotic course even if feeling better
See doctor if symptoms don't improve within 12-24 hours of starting antibiotics

symptoms: painful, tender, fluctuant lump in breast
erythema and swelling over the lump
guidance: Seek medical care immediately. Ultrasound confirms abscess. Treatment: needle aspiration or incision and drainage. Continue breastfeeding on the unaffected side; the affected side can be pumped (but empty the breast). Antibiotics are needed.
precautions: Do not delay treatment of mastitis
Keep the breast empty to prevent abscess

symptoms: sleep disturbances (unable to sleep even when baby sleeps)
thoughts of harming baby or self
guidance: This is a psychiatric emergency. Requires immediate hospitalization and medication. Postpartum psychosis is rare but serious — risk is higher in women with a history of bipolar disorder. Do not leave the mother alone with the baby until treated. Treatment: antipsychotics, mood stabilizers, and hospitalization.
precautions: Secure the baby with another caregiver

symptoms: continuous uncontrollable leaking of urine or stool from vagina
inability to control urination or defecation
occurs after prolonged difficult labor or birth injury
guidance: Obstetric fistula is caused by prolonged obstructed labor, mostly preventable by timely C-section. It is fully curable with surgery. Free surgical repair is available at government hospitals under the National Health Mission. Counseling and support groups help women cope with stigma and isolation. Report cases to district hospital.
precautions: Prevent by delivering in hospital — obstructed labor managed by C-section prevents fistula
Girls should not marry or become pregnant before age 18
Seek care at district hospital — do not hide condition due to stigma
Proper skin care with petroleum jelly prevents pressure sores
Surgery has over 90% success rate — full recovery is possible

symptoms: pink-red rash starting on face spreading to body
swollen lymph nodes behind ears and neck
in fetus: congenital rubella syndrome — deafness, heart defects, vision loss, intellectual disability
guidance: Rubella in the first trimester causes severe birth defects (Congenital Rubella Syndrome) in up to 90% of cases. Vaccination before pregnancy is the only prevention. If contracted in pregnancy, seek immediate specialist care. Women of childbearing age should check vaccination status and get MMR vaccine before conceiving.
precautions: Get MMR (measles-mumps-rubella) vaccine before pregnancy if not already vaccinated
Do NOT get MMR vaccine during pregnancy — avoid pregnancy for 1 month after vaccination
Avoid contact with anyone who has measles or rubella during pregnancy
All children should receive 2 doses of MMR under the Universal Immunization Programme
Report any rash during pregnancy immediately to doctor

symptoms: abnormal vaginal bleeding (between periods, after sex, after menopause)
early stages often have NO symptoms
guidance: Cervical cancer is almost entirely preventable. Free cervical cancer screening (VIA — Visual Inspection with Acetic Acid) is available at PHCs and CHCs under NPCDCS. HPV vaccine available for girls age 9-14 at government schools. Early-stage cervical cancer is curable. All women aged 30-65 should be screened every 5 years.
precautions: Get screened — free VIA screening at nearest PHC or CHC
HPV vaccination for girls age 9-14 before sexual debut
Report any abnormal vaginal bleeding to a doctor immediately
Do not ignore any symptoms due to stigma or embarrassment
Smoking increases cervical cancer risk — avoid tobacco

symptoms: lower back pain that is dull or rhythmic
rupture of membranes (water breaking) before 37 weeks
guidance: If you have signs of preterm labor, go to the hospital immediately. Tocolytics (to stop contractions) and corticosteroids (to mature fetal lungs) are given. Prevention: good ANC, avoid smoking, treat infections, bed rest if cervical insufficiency.
precautions: Seek care immediately for contractions before 37 weeks
Attend all ANC visits for cervical monitoring

symptoms: sudden gush or continuous trickle of fluid from vagina
fluid is clear or slightly blood-tinged
no pain associated with fluid loss
may be accompanied by infection (fever, foul-smelling discharge)
guidance: Go to the hospital immediately. There is a risk of cord prolapse, infection, and preterm labor. If term (≥37 weeks), induction is usually done. If preterm, management depends on gestational age and infection status. Monitor for signs of chorioamnionitis.
precautions: Do not use tampons or have sex after membrane rupture
Antibiotics may be given if infection risk

symptoms: sometimes no symptoms in early stages
guidance: Immediate antibiotics (IV) and prompt delivery. It is a major cause of maternal sepsis and neonatal infection. Do not delay delivery once diagnosed. Usually occurs with prolonged rupture of membranes or prolonged labor.

symptoms: vaginal bleeding after 20 weeks of pregnancy
may be painless (placenta previa) or painful (placental abruption)
bleeding can be light to heavy
guidance: Any vaginal bleeding in the second half of pregnancy is an emergency. Go to the hospital immediately. Do not do a vaginal examination at home. Causes: placenta previa, placental abruption, cervical polyps. Ultrasound to locate the placenta. Treatment depends on cause and severity.
precautions: Do not ignore bleeding — seek care immediately
Do not have sexual intercourse if placenta previa is diagnosed
In case of abruption, immediate C-section may be needed

symptoms: painless bright red vaginal bleeding in second or third trimester
guidance: Diagnosis by ultrasound. Management: rest, avoid intercourse, and no vaginal exams. If bleeding is heavy or at term, C-section is required. In mild cases, admission for monitoring and corticosteroids to mature fetal lungs. Emergency blood transfusion may be needed.
precautions: Avoid sex if placenta previa is diagnosed
Immediate hospital evaluation for any bleeding
Deliver at a facility with blood bank and C-section capability

guidance: Medical emergency. Immediate delivery is often needed. Management: IV fluids, blood transfusion, and emergency C-section. Abruption can cause maternal and fetal death. Risk factors: hypertension, trauma, smoking, cocaine use.
precautions: Seek care for sudden abdominal pain in late pregnancy

symptoms: fetus may be easily palpable (abnormal position)
guidance: Life-threatening emergency. Requires immediate emergency laparotomy and repair or hysterectomy. Most common in women with previous C-section scars. Prevention: avoid unnecessary C-sections, vaginal birth after C-section (VBAC) should be in a hospital with immediate surgical backup.
precautions: Avoid unsupervised vaginal delivery with previous C-section

symptoms: head delivers but shoulders are stuck behind pubic symphysis
inability to deliver shoulders after head
requires specific maneuvers (McRoberts, suprapubic pressure, Woods screw)
guidance: This is an obstetric emergency. The delivery team will perform maneuvers. Prevent: avoid excessive fetal weight (gestational diabetes control), and assess for risk factors (fetal macrosomia, maternal diabetes, prolonged labor). If diagnosed, specific emergency maneuvers are needed.
precautions: Do not pull on the head

symptoms: visualization or palpation of cord in the vagina after membrane rupture
fetal heart rate abnormalities (variable or prolonged decelerations)
guidance: Emergency. Relieve pressure on the cord by elevating the presenting part (hand in vagina), place mother in Trendelenburg or knee-chest position. Immediate delivery (often C-section) is needed. Do not attempt to push cord back in. Call for emergency help.
precautions: Avoid artificial rupture of membranes if presenting part is not engaged
If cord prolapse occurs, call for immediate help
Maintain pressure on presenting part until delivery

symptoms: occurs during labor, delivery, or immediately postpartum
guidance: This is a rare but catastrophic emergency. Immediate cardiopulmonary resuscitation, oxygenation, IV fluids, and treatment of DIC. Requires intensive care. Most deaths occur within 1 hour. Survival is low, but prompt intensive care improves outcomes.
precautions: No specific prevention — rare and unpredictable

symptoms: delayed expulsion of placenta (>30 minutes after delivery)
guidance: Manual removal of placenta under anesthesia is required. If heavy bleeding, it is an emergency. Prevent with active management of the third stage of labor (oxytocin). Delayed recognition leads to PPH.
precautions: If retained, call for skilled assistance

symptoms: tear of perineum during delivery (1st, 2nd, 3rd, or 4th degree)
guidance: Repair under local or regional anesthesia. For 3rd/4th degree tears, repair by an experienced surgeon. Good wound care: sitz baths, pain relief. Prevent episiotomy only if needed; perineal massage during pregnancy can reduce tears.

symptoms: bleeding after delivery that is not due to uterine atony or retained products
guidance: Suturing of cervical tear under good visualization. Prevent by avoiding rapid and forceful deliveries. Monitor for bleeding and infection.
precautions: Inspect cervix for tears after delivery

symptoms: severe pain in perineum or vagina after delivery
guidance: Surgical evacuation of hematoma and control of bleeding. Analgesia. Some small hematomas may be managed conservatively. Prevent by avoiding trauma during delivery and good hemostasis after episiotomy.

symptoms: inability to urinate after vaginal delivery (within 6 hours)
guidance: Catheterization may be needed. Preventive measures: encourage early ambulation, provide privacy for voiding, and avoid excessive fluids in early postpartum. If retention persists, bladder training.

Treat with broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (gentamicin + clindamycin or ampicillin). May need to add metronidazole. Usually caused by retained placental fragments or prolonged labor. Prevention: sterile delivery techniques.

symptoms: redness, swelling, pain, discharge from C-section wound
guidance: Wound care, antibiotics, and sometimes surgical drainage. Good hygiene, keep wound dry, and early detection. Risk factors: obesity, diabetes, emergency C-section.
Can present with hyperthyroid then hypothyroid phase. Often self-limiting. If hypothyroid, may need levothyroxine. Monitor TSH. Usually resolves within 12 months.
Frequent and effective breastfeeding or pumping. Apply cold compresses after feeding, warm before feeding. Supportive bra. If not resolved, can progress to mastitis. Avoid stopping feeds.

Ensure correct latch and positioning. Use expressed breast milk on nipple, let air dry. Hydrogel pads or nipple cream. If fungal (thrush), antifungal treatment for mother and baby. Do not stop breastfeeding.

symptoms: painless or slightly tender lump in the breast
guidance: Ultrasound to confirm. Continue breastfeeding to empty the breast. If persistent, aspiration may be needed. Reassure that it is benign.

category: Diastasis Recti (Separation of Abdominal Muscles) in Pregnancy
symptoms: visible bulge or ridge in the midline of the abdomen when straining
guidance: Postpartum exercises to strengthen the core (e.g., pelvic tilts, deep abdominal contractions). Avoid heavy lifting and sit-ups that worsen separation. Most resolve within 6-12 months.

symptoms: tingling, numbness, or pain in fingers (thumb, index, middle)
guidance: Wrist splints at night, avoid repetitive wrist movements, elevate hands. Usually resolves after delivery. If severe, local corticosteroid injection may be used.

symptoms: high blood pressure after 20 weeks without proteinuria
guidance: Monitor BP regularly. Salt restriction, rest. If BP > 160/110, antihypertensives (labetalol, methyldopa). Close monitoring for progression to preeclampsia.
precautions: Watch for warning signs of preeclampsia
Do not stop antihypertensives without advice

symptoms: usually associated with deep vein thrombosis (leg pain, swelling)
guidance: Medical emergency. Call 108. Immediate anticoagulation (LMWH) and supportive care. Risk is higher in pregnancy and postpartum. Prevent with early mobilization, compression stockings, and anticoagulation in high-risk.
precautions: Do not ignore leg swelling or chest pain

symptoms: pain, swelling, redness, and warmth in one leg (usually calf or thigh)
guidance: Urgent Doppler ultrasound. Treatment: therapeutic anticoagulation (LMWH). Prevent by compression stockings and early mobility. DVT can lead to PE.
precautions: Seek care for leg swelling and pain

symptoms: pain radiating to the groin or inner thighs
guidance: Pelvic support belts, avoid asymmetrical movements (stairs, getting in/out of car). Rest, physical therapy. Usually resolves postpartum. Use of crutches in severe cases.

symptoms: painful, swollen veins around the anus
guidance: Prevent constipation with high-fiber diet and adequate fluids. Topical creams (hydrocortisone, witch hazel), cold compresses, and sitz baths. Usually resolves postpartum.
precautions: Do not use laxatives without advice

symptoms: swollen, twisted veins in legs (blue or purple)
guidance: Elevate legs, wear compression stockings, avoid prolonged standing. Exercise (walking) helps. Rarely, thrombosis can occur.

category: Obstetric Cholestasis (Intrahepatic Cholestasis of Pregnancy — ICP)
symptoms: severe itching (pruritus) especially on palms and soles, worse at night
guidance: This is a high-risk condition — can lead to fetal distress and stillbirth. Report itching immediately. Diagnosis: elevated bile acids. Treatment: ursodeoxycholic acid, monitoring fetal well-being, and early delivery (often at 37-38 weeks).
Medical emergency. Immediate delivery is required. Supportive care: correction of coagulation, glucose, and liver failure. Liver transplant may be needed. Early recognition is crucial.
precautions: Suspect if liver enzymes elevated with coagulopathy

category: HELLP Syndrome (Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets)
guidance: Medical emergency. Immediate delivery is the definitive treatment. Corticosteroids may improve platelets. Transfusion for severe thrombocytopenia. Monitor liver and renal function.
precautions: Suspect in preeclampsia with epigastric pain
Immediate lab testing (hemolysis, liver enzymes, platelets)

category: Pregestational Diabetes (Type 1 or Type 2 in Pregnancy)
guidance: Preconception care: optimize glycemic control (HbA1c < 6.5%) before pregnancy. During pregnancy: tight glucose control, frequent monitoring, insulin (Type 1 and often Type 2), and fetal surveillance. High risk of macrosomia, preeclampsia, and stillbirth.
Monitor BP regularly. No treatment unless BP > 160/110. Delivery at 37 weeks if no progression. Watch for preeclampsia warning signs.

symptoms: risk of macrosomia, oligohydramnios, fetal distress
guidance: Induction of labor is recommended after 41 weeks to prevent complications. Fetal monitoring (BPP, NST). Prevent by accurate dating and timely induction.

symptoms: fundal height smaller than gestational age
guidance: Diagnosed by ultrasound (AFI < 5 cm). Management: increased hydration (oral or IV), close fetal monitoring, and consider delivery if compromised. In term, induction is often recommended.

Ultrasound diagnosis (AFI > 25 cm). Causes include fetal anomaly, maternal diabetes, or idiopathic. Management: treat underlying cause, amnioreduction if severe, or NSAIDs to reduce fluid. Monitor for preterm labor.

High-risk pregnancy. Needs frequent ANC, ultrasound for chorionicity, growth monitoring, and cervical length measurement. Delivery often preterm. Discuss mode of delivery. Extra folic acid and iron are needed.

symptoms: may be with or without infection
guidance: Hospital admission. Corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity, antibiotics for infection, and close monitoring for chorioamnionitis. Delivery if signs of infection or fetal distress. Prolonged PPROM can lead to cord compression.

symptoms: painless cervical dilation in second trimester
guidance: Diagnosis by transvaginal ultrasound (cervical length < 25 mm before 24 weeks). Cerclage (stitch) is used if indicated. Progesterone supplementation. Close monitoring.

symptoms: high BP before pregnancy or before 20 weeks
risk of preeclampsia and fetal growth restriction
guidance: Continue antihypertensives (avoid ACE inhibitors, ARBs; use labetalol, methyldopa). Monitor for superimposed preeclampsia. Frequent growth scans.

symptoms: fundal height < 2 cm below gestational age
guidance: Identify cause: preeclampsia, placental insufficiency, infections, smoking. Serial growth scans and Doppler. Manage hypertension. Delivery if fetal distress or severe growth restriction (often before term).
If suspected, avoid post-term pregnancy. Consider elective C-section if estimated fetal weight > 4.5 kg (especially with diabetes). Control maternal blood sugar to prevent.
precautions: Avoid excessive weight gain in pregnancy

guidance: Medical emergency. Immediate IV antibiotics, IV fluids, vasopressors, and source control. ICU care. Early recognition and treatment reduce mortality.
precautions: Screen for sepsis in febrile postpartum women

symptoms: bleeding from puncture sites, gums, wound, vagina
laboratory: low platelets, high PT/APTT, low fibrinogen
guidance: Occurs with placental abruption, amniotic fluid embolism, sepsis, PPH. Treat the underlying cause. Supportive: blood products (platelets, FFP, cryoprecipitate).

symptoms: seizures occurring within 48 hours to 6 weeks postpartum
guidance: Treatment: magnesium sulfate. Continue for 24 hours. Antihypertensives if needed. Monitor for underlying causes (stroke, epilepsy).

symptoms: occurs in last month of pregnancy or up to 5 months postpartum
guidance: Echocardiography for diagnosis. Treatment: heart failure management (diuretics, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, beta-blockers), bromocriptine may help. Prognosis is variable. Do not get pregnant again if LV function not recovered.

Give Rh immunoglobulin (anti-D) at 28 weeks and within 72 hours of any bleeding, abortion, or delivery. If already sensitized, monitor fetal MCA Doppler for anemia and consider intrauterine transfusions.
precautions: Know blood group in first trimester
Give anti-D after any bleeding episode

guidance: Screen for asymptomatic bacteriuria at 12-16 weeks (urine culture). Treat with safe antibiotics (nitrofurantoin, amoxicillin, cephalosporins). Pyelonephritis requires hospitalization and IV antibiotics.
precautions: Prevent with good hydration and hygiene

guidance: Normalize feelings but if excessive, seek counseling. Relaxation techniques, mindfulness, and CBT. Support from family. If severe, medication (SSRIs like sertraline) may be safe under supervision.

symptoms: sharp pain radiating from lower back down the leg
often due to pressure on sciatic nerve
guidance: Gentle stretching, warm packs, and good posture. Side-lying with pillows between knees. Physiotherapy. Usually resolves postpartum.
Avoid iron supplements unless indicated. Monitor serum ferritin. Phlebotomy may be needed. Genetic counseling.

Thyroid hormone replacement (levothyroxine) is essential. Dose often increases during pregnancy. Monitor TSH every 4-6 weeks. Untreated hypothyroidism increases risk of fetal neurodevelopmental issues.
precautions: Check thyroid before and during pregnancy

guidance: Antithyroid drugs (PTU in first trimester, methimazole in second) are used. Avoid radioactive iodine. Monitor fetal thyroid (maternal antibodies can cross). Surgery for severe cases after first trimester.
precautions: Treat with PTU in first trimester

guidance: Screen all pregnant women for HBsAg. If positive, give baby HBIG and Hepatitis B vaccine within 12 hours of birth. If viral load > 200,000 IU/mL, start antiviral (tenofovir) in third trimester.
precautions: Breastfeeding is safe if baby vaccinated

guidance: Screen if risk factors. No vaccine. No treatment during pregnancy (DAAs not yet approved in pregnancy). Monitor liver function. Baby tested at 18 months. Breastfeeding is safe.

symptoms: risk to fetus: congenital varicella syndrome (limb hypoplasia, skin scarring, eye defects) if infection in early pregnancy
guidance: If exposed and non-immune, give VZIG within 96 hours. If infected, treat with acyclovir. Severe cases require hospitalization. Prevent by vaccinating women before pregnancy (avoid pregnancy for 1 month after vaccine).

symptoms: fever, cough, body aches, fatigue, sore throat
pregnancy increases risk of severe disease (pneumonia, ICU admission)
guidance: Antiviral (oseltamivir) should be started as soon as possible, regardless of vaccination status. Flu vaccine is safe and recommended in pregnancy (any trimester).

symptoms: fever, rash, joint pain, red eyes
risk of microcephaly and other birth defects
guidance: Avoid travel to Zika-endemic areas during pregnancy. Use mosquito repellent. If exposure, fetal ultrasound and amniocentesis may be considered. No specific treatment.

symptoms: congenital: hydrocephalus, calcifications, chorioretinitis, intellectual disability
guidance: Prevent: avoid raw/undercooked meat, wash vegetables, and avoid cat litter. If seroconversion in pregnancy, treat with spiramycin (early) or pyrimethamine+sulfadiazine (late) to reduce fetal infection.

symptoms: congenital: hearing loss, intellectual disability, microcephaly
guidance: Prevent: avoid sharing food/utensils with young children, handwashing. Antiviral (valganciclovir) for neonatal treatment. No proven prevention of vertical transmission.
precautions: Avoid saliva contact with young children
Monitor fetus if primary infection in pregnancy

symptoms: fetal: risk of hydrops fetalis (severe anemia) if infected in first half of pregnancy
guidance: If exposed, test for IgG/IgM. If acute, monitor fetal MCA Doppler for anemia. Intrauterine transfusion for severe fetal anemia. Most infections do not cause adverse outcomes.
precautions: Avoid exposure to infected children if non-immune

symptoms: fever, muscle aches, sometimes GI symptoms
fetal: abortion, premature delivery, neonatal sepsis
guidance: Avoid foods: unpasteurized dairy, deli meats, raw sprouts, soft cheeses. If infection, treat with ampicillin + gentamicin. Early treatment improves outcomes.

symptoms: cough > 2 weeks, fever, night sweats, weight loss
can cause preterm labor and low birth weight
guidance: Screen with chest X-ray (protected) and GeneXpert. Treatment: standard anti-TB drugs (rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol, pyrazinamide) are safe in pregnancy. Breastfeeding is allowed on treatment.
precautions: TB is not a reason for termination

symptoms: can cause severe anemia, preterm labor, low birth weight, maternal death
guidance: Prompt diagnosis (RDT, microscopy) and treatment. Treat with antimalarials (artemisinin combinations are safe in 2nd and 3rd trimester). Prevention: use insecticide-treated nets and chemoprophylaxis in high-risk areas.

symptoms: high fever, headache, joint pain, rash
risk of severe dengue (plasma leakage, hemorrhage)
can cause preterm labor, abruptio placentae
guidance: Supportive care: hydration, paracetamol for fever. Avoid NSAIDs. Hospitalization for monitoring. Maintain hydration. No antiviral.

symptoms: fever, rash, joint pain, red eyes
risk of microcephaly and other birth defects
guidance: Avoid travel to Zika-endemic areas during pregnancy. Use mosquito repellent. If exposure, fetal ultrasound and amniocentesis may be considered. No specific treatment.

symptoms: prolonged fever, headache, constipation/diarrhea, abdominal pain, rose spots
guidance: Treat with azithromycin or ceftriaxone (safe in pregnancy). Avoid chloramphenicol (risk of gray baby syndrome). Hydration and nutrition. Prevent with food and water hygiene.

symptoms: acute hepatitis: fever, nausea, vomiting, jaundice, dark urine
particularly severe in third trimester (fulminant hepatitis, mortality 20-30%)
guidance: Supportive care. Pregnant women with HEV need hospitalization. There is no specific antiviral. Prevention: safe water, hygiene. No vaccine widely available in India.
precautions: Pregnant women should avoid travel to HEV endemic areas

symptoms: abdominal pain (may be in right lower quadrant, but location varies with gestational age)
laboratory: leukocytosis (normal in pregnancy, so difficult)
guidance: Surgical emergency. Laparoscopic appendectomy is safe in pregnancy. Delay increases risk of perforation and peritonitis. Do not delay imaging (ultrasound/MRI).
precautions: Suspect appendicitis in any acute abdomen

guidance: Diagnosis: elevated lipase/amylase. Treatment: supportive (IV fluids, pain relief, fasting). Gallstone pancreatitis may need endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP). Hyperlipidemia requires lipid-lowering and diet.

symptoms: risk factors: previous DVT/PE, thrombophilia, immobility, obesity, preeclampsia
guidance: Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) prophylaxis is given to high-risk women. Usually started in pregnancy and continued for 6 weeks postpartum. Dose based on weight.

symptoms: renal colic: severe flank pain radiating to groin
guidance: Ultrasound is first-line imaging. Management: hydration, pain relief (opioids safe), and if obstructed, may need ureteral stent or ureteroscopy. Most pass spontaneously.
Diagnosis: sleep study. Treatment: CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure) is safe. Weight gain exacerbates. May increase risk of preeclampsia.
precautions: If symptoms, refer for sleep study

symptoms: PUPPP (pruritic urticarial papules and plaques of pregnancy): itchy, red, hive-like rash on stretch marks
guidance: Most are benign and resolve postpartum. Treatment: topical corticosteroids, antihistamines, emollients. PUPPP usually starts on the abdomen and spreads.
precautions: Reassurance that it resolves after delivery

symptoms: may be due to obstetric cholestasis (bile acids)
or due to dry skin, cholestasis
guidance: If itching without rash, rule out obstetric cholestasis by checking bile acids and liver function. If negative, treat with emollients and antihistamines.

symptoms: worse after meals or lying down
guidance: Avoid large meals, spicy/fried foods, eat small frequent meals. Don't lie down immediately after eating. Antacids (calcium carbonate) and ranitidine (safe) or omeprazole if needed.

symptoms: often due to hormonal changes and iron supplements
guidance: Increase fiber (fruits, vegetables, whole grains), drink plenty of water, exercise. Stool softeners (docusate) and laxatives (lactulose) are safe if needed. Do not use stimulant laxatives.

symptoms: leakage of urine with cough, sneeze, laugh, or exercise
guidance: Pelvic floor exercises (Kegels) help. Avoid heavy lifting. Most resolves postpartum, but may persist. If persistent, physiotherapy and sometimes surgery.
precautions: Do not ignore — it can be treated

guidance: Ultrasound is the first-line imaging (mammography is safe but rarely needed). Biopsy if suspicious. Most are benign. Reassurance.

symptoms: pain in the pelvis (front or back)
guidance: Physiotherapy, pelvic support belts, gentle exercise. Avoid asymmetric activities. Usually resolves postpartum.

symptoms: risk of placental abruption, preterm labor, fracture
guidance: Seek medical evaluation after any fall, especially if abdominal pain, bleeding, or decreased fetal movements. Monitor for uterine contractions.
Screen all pregnant women for domestic violence. Offer safety planning, counseling, and referral to shelters and legal aid. If in immediate danger, call helplines (1091, 181).

category: Substance Use in Pregnancy (Alcohol, Tobacco, Drugs)
guidance: Counseling and cessation support. Tobacco: nicotine replacement. Alcohol: complete abstinence. Opioid dependence: methadone or buprenorphine maintenance. Neonatal abstinence syndrome requires special care.

symptoms: polyhydramnios in one sac, oligohydramnios in the other
guidance: Refer to fetal medicine specialist. Treatment options: amnioreduction, laser ablation of placental vessels, or septostomy. Monitored closely.

symptoms: only one artery in the cord
may be associated with fetal anomalies or growth restriction
guidance: Usually an isolated finding with no clinical significance. But need to check for fetal anomalies and growth. Monitor growth and do anomaly scan.

category: Velamentous Cord Insertion and Vasa Previa
symptoms: cord inserts into membranes, not the placenta
vasa previa: fetal vessels cross over the cervical os
risk of fetal hemorrhage with membrane rupture
guidance: Diagnosed by ultrasound (color Doppler). Vasa previa requires elective C-section before rupture of membranes. Velamentous insertion may increase risk of growth restriction.

symptoms: not a disease but a procedure for cervical insufficiency
guidance: Cerclage is placed between 12-16 weeks. Monitor for infection and preterm labor. Remove at 37 weeks. Bed rest may be recommended.
Offer for chromosomal anomalies, neural tube defects, Rh disease. Counseling about risks and benefits. Procedure under ultrasound guidance.

symptoms: procedure for early genetic testing (10-13 weeks)
guidance: Offer for genetic disorders. Transabdominal or transcervical. Rh-negative receive RhoGAM. Ultrasound guided. Results in 1-2 weeks.

symptoms: mother blood group O, baby A or B
risk of hemolytic disease of newborn (usually mild)
guidance: Usually mild. Monitor newborn for jaundice. Phototherapy if needed. Rarely severe. No prenatal treatment needed.
precautions: Blood group testing of mother and father

symptoms: not a disease, a test to detect fetal red cells in maternal circulation
used in Rh-negative mothers after trauma/bleeding
guidance: Done in Rh-negative women after any antenatal hemorrhage, trauma, or abdominal injury. Determines the amount of RhIg needed.

symptoms: procedure to turn baby to head-down
guidance: ECV is attempted at 37 weeks under ultrasound guidance. Success rate 50-60%. Tocolytics may be given. If failed, C-section is planned.
precautions: No vaginal delivery of breech without expertise

symptoms: trial of labor after previous C-section
guidance: VBAC is safe in selected women. Contraindications: classical scar, >2 previous C-sections, placenta previa. Use continuous fetal monitoring. Have emergency readiness.

symptoms: procedure to induce or augment labor
guidance: Done when cervix is favorable. Monitor for cord prolapse and meconium. If not in labor, induction may be needed.

symptoms: surgical cut in perineum during delivery
to prevent severe tears or expedite delivery
guidance: Use only when indicated (fetal distress, shoulder dystocia, assisted vaginal delivery). Restrictive use reduces postpartum pain and perineal trauma.

symptoms: use of vacuum cup to aid delivery
indications: prolonged second stage, fetal distress, maternal exhaustion
guidance: Requires trained provider. Contraindications: prematurity (<34 weeks), breech, face presentation. Risk of cephalohematoma and scalp laceration.
Used in selected cases. Requires skilled operator. For outlet/midpelvic. C-section is alternative.

category: Fetal Scalp Electrode and Intrauterine Pressure Catheter
symptoms: used for more accurate fetal heart rate and contraction pressure
guidance: Used when external monitoring is inadequate. Require ruptured membranes and cervical dilation. Risk of infection and scalp injury.
